title: Secrets and API keys
plain: A secret is a value that proves you may use a service, like an API key or a password. Keep real secrets in a .env file that Git ignores. Commit only .env.example with fake values.
check: Your app needs an API key. Where do you put the real value, what do you commit instead, and which command proves that Git will ignore the real one?
rubric: Runs git ls-files with secret-type names and reads the result: nothing printed is the goal.
Creates .env with a made-up value and .env.example with the same name and a placeholder.
Shows that .env is ignored by running git check-ignore -v .env.
try: In your project run git ls-files .env "*.env" "*.pem" "*.key". It lists the files that Git tracks and whose names suggest secrets. Nothing printed is the goal. If a name appears, do not open or paste the file: continue with the rotating-a-leaked-key card. Then create a file .env with the single line DEMO_KEY=not-a-real-key (use your editor) and run git check-ignore -v .env. It prints the rule that hides the file, for example .gitignore:1:.env followed by .env. If nothing prints, .env is not ignored yet.
pitfall: Wrong belief: adding .env to .gitignore also fixes a key I already committed. Correct: .gitignore only affects files that Git does not track yet. A committed key stays in the history and must be replaced.

title: Rotating a leaked key
plain: Rotating a key means making a new key and revoking (disabling) the old one at the service that issued it. Do it first when a key is exposed: deleting the file does not stop misuse.
check: You pasted a real API key into a chat an hour ago. In which order do you do these four things, and why: delete the chat message, revoke the key, look at the provider's usage page, put a new key into .env?
rubric: Puts the steps in order: revoke the old key at the provider, check usage and bills, make a new key, store it in .env and in the hosting settings, remove the old value from files, and rewrite history last and only if needed.
Lists every place the key is used, found with git grep -l, so that none keeps the old value.
Refers to the key as the key and never types its value.
try: In your project run git grep -l -i -E "api[_-]?key". It prints only the names of files that mention a key, never the key itself. For each file, note where the real value comes from: .env, a hosting setting or the code itself. These are the places to update after a rotation. Then open your key provider's key page, find the Revoke (or Delete) button and the Create button, and press neither: this step is only a plan.
pitfall: Wrong belief: deleting the key from the file, deleting the repository or force-pushing makes a leaked key safe. Correct: copies, forks, caches and chat logs can keep the value, so the service that issued the key must revoke it. Rewriting history is the last, optional step.

title: Two-factor sign-in
plain: Two-factor authentication (2FA) asks for a second proof besides your password. The proof can be a code from an authenticator app or a security key. A stolen password alone is then not enough.
check: Why is your e-mail account usually the first one to protect with 2FA, and what could an attacker do with it?
rubric: Lists the accounts that matter most: e-mail, GitHub, your AI provider, your hosting and your domain registrar.
Turns on a second factor for at least one of them, preferring an authenticator app or a security key to text messages.
Stores the recovery codes in a password manager or on paper, not in a project folder or in chat.
try: Write a list of five accounts that would hurt most to lose, e-mail first. For each one, open its security settings and note whether a second factor is on, and which kind. Turn it on for the first account that has none, using an authenticator app, and save the recovery codes in a password manager or on paper. Never type a password or code into this chat.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a strong password is enough, and a code sent by text message is as safe as an app. Correct: passwords leak in breaches, and a second factor means a leaked password alone does not open the account. Text messages are the weakest second factor, because phone numbers can be taken over. A passkey goes further: it replaces the password with a key kept on your device.

title: Secrets and Codex
plain: Codex can read files in your project, including .env. A deny rule in a beta permissions profile can block reads of matching files, such as **/*.env. Chat history is saved on your computer too.
check: You set a deny rule for .env in a permissions profile. By which route could Codex still get to the secret, and what would you do about it?
rubric: Names the setting: a permissions profile with a deny rule for **/*.env, and says it replaces the sandbox_mode setting.
Says the rule covers the commands Codex runs, not text pasted into the chat, so a pasted key must still be revoked.
Says a deny rule is one layer only; secrets belong in a .env file that Git ignores, and the sandbox limits writes.
try: Create a file .env with one line: DEMO_KEY=not-a-real-key. Read the permissions page at https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/permissions.md (checked 2026-10-08) and find the example that sets **/*.env to deny. Write two lines in your own words: what it blocks, and what it does not block. Do not add it yet: the profile replaces the sandbox_mode line in .codex/config.toml, so ask your tutor first.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a deny rule makes my secrets invisible to the AI. Correct: it covers only the commands Codex runs, not text you paste yourself. Keep secrets in .env, and rotate any key you pasted.

title: Storing passwords
plain: A password hash is a value computed from a password that cannot be reversed. A slow algorithm such as Argon2id or bcrypt, with a unique salt, makes it. Store only the hash.
check: Two users choose the same password, and each gets a unique salt. How will their stored hashes compare, and what does that stop an attacker from doing?
rubric: Says the two stored hashes differ, because each user has a different salt.
Says this stops an attacker from spotting users who share a password and from using one precomputed table of hashes against all users.
Says the hash must also be slow and come from a proven library (Argon2id, bcrypt), because a fast hash such as SHA-256 lets an attacker test very many guesses per second.
try: Run python3 -c "import hashlib; print(hashlib.sha256(b'hello').hexdigest())" twice (python on Windows). Both runs print the same 64 characters, starting with 2cf24dba: equal input gives equal output. Now change b'hello' to b'x1hello' and then to b'x2hello'. The results look completely different. That is what a salt does. Real passwords need a slow algorithm from a library such as bcrypt or Argon2id, not SHA-256.
pitfall: Wrong belief: hashing passwords with MD5 or SHA-256 is safe enough, or a login that I write myself is fine. Correct: fast hashes let attackers test many guesses quickly. Use the slow, salted password hashing of your framework or a login service.

title: Authentication and authorization
plain: Authentication checks who you are, for example with a password. Authorization checks what you are allowed to do afterwards. Being logged in does not mean you may see or change everything.
check: A logged-in user changes /orders/17 to /orders/18 in the address bar and sees someone else's order. Which of the two ideas failed, and where must the fix be made?
rubric: Says authentication worked (the server knows who the user is) and authorization failed (nothing checked who owns order 18).
Puts the fix on the server: for every request, look up the order and compare its owner with the logged-in user, and refuse with 403 (or 404) if they differ.
Does not rely on hiding the link or on a check inside the web page, because anyone can type or send another address.
try: Run curl -i https://api.github.com/user (in Windows PowerShell type curl.exe instead of curl). The first line contains the status 401 (often written 401 Unauthorized) and the body says Requires authentication: the server does not know who you are, so authentication is missing. Predict which status a server sends when you ARE logged in but not allowed to open a page (the usual answer is 403), and why that is a different problem.
pitfall: Wrong belief: if a page needs a login, all the data on it is protected. Correct: a login only proves who you are. The server must also check, on every request, that this user may use this item, because anyone can change an address or send a request without your page.

title: HTTPS
plain: HTTPS is HTTP with encryption (TLS). It stops other people on the network from reading or changing what travels between a browser and a server. The server proves its identity with a certificate.
check: A phishing site starts with https:// and your browser shows a padlock or a similar secure sign. What does that sign actually guarantee, and what does it not guarantee?
rubric: Says the connection is encrypted and the certificate matches the website's domain name.
Says it does not prove the site is honest: a fake site can also have a padlock.
Says plain http:// sends text that others on the network can read or change, such as passwords.
try: Run curl -I https://example.com (in Windows PowerShell type curl.exe). The first line starts with HTTP and shows the status 200: the request travelled through an encrypted TLS connection that curl checked. Then run curl -I https://expired.badssl.com/, a public test site with an expired certificate. curl stops with an error that says the certificate has expired and prints no page. Nothing on your computer changes.
pitfall: Wrong belief: a padlock means a website is safe, and a certificate error is an annoying warning that I can switch off. Correct: the padlock only means an encrypted connection to that domain name. Turning off certificate checks, for example with curl -k, removes the protection against someone pretending to be the server.

title: Cross-site scripting (XSS)
plain: Cross-site scripting (XSS) happens when a page shows text typed by a user as HTML or JavaScript. An attacker's script then runs in other visitors' browsers. Show user text as text, not as HTML.
check: A comment box saves what visitors type and shows it to everyone. What could happen if a visitor types an HTML tag that contains a script, and which line of page code would you change so the text is shown as plain text?
rubric: Finds the line that turns user text into HTML (innerHTML).
Explains that the browser would run the code in the onerror attribute of an img tag for every visitor.
Fixes it with textContent, or with the framework's default escaping.
pitfall: Wrong belief: XSS only matters on big sites, and checking the form is enough. Correct: any page that shows user text can be attacked, and the fix belongs where the text is shown: output it as text, not HTML, and keep your framework's default escaping on.

title: Validating input
plain: Validating input means checking, in server code, that data from users has the expected type, length and format. Reject everything else. Do not trust any data that comes from outside your program.
check: Your signup form checks in the browser that age is a number from 13 to 120. Why is that not enough, and where must the same check also exist?
rubric: Writes down what is allowed for the field: type, length, range or a fixed list.
Puts the check in server code, not only in the browser form.
Rejects bad input with a clear message and does not repeat it back as HTML.
pitfall: Wrong belief: checks in the browser form protect my server. Correct: anyone can send requests without your page, so the server must check every input itself. Prefer an allow-list (accept what you expect) to a block-list (reject known bad words).

title: Least privilege
plain: Least privilege means giving a person, key or program only the access it needs for its job, and nothing more. If it is stolen or makes a mistake, the damage stays small.
check: A script only needs to read recipe data. Which two limits could you put on its database login or token, and what does each limit prevent?
rubric: Names the job of one key, token or program and the smallest access that still does the job (read or write, one repository or all, one table or all).
Narrows it, for example by opening a database read-only, and shows that a write is refused.
Says what the broad version could have damaged if it had leaked.
try: Use the practice.db file from the SQL basics card, or make one: python3 -m sqlite3 practice.db (Python 3.12 or newer), then type CREATE TABLE todo (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT, done INTEGER); and INSERT INTO todo (title, done) VALUES ('buy milk', 0); and .quit. Now run python3 -c "import sqlite3; c=sqlite3.connect('file:practice.db?mode=ro', uri=True); print(c.execute('SELECT * FROM todo').fetchall()); c.execute('DELETE FROM todo')" (python on Windows). The SELECT prints the rows, and the DELETE stops with the error attempt to write a readonly database. A program that only reads should connect this way.
pitfall: Wrong belief: giving a key full access is easier, so it is fine for a small project. Correct: a leaked broad key lets an attacker do everything you can do, and a narrow key limits the damage. Start with read-only or one-repository access and widen it only when a task needs it.

title: Package safety
plain: Every package you install is code from strangers that runs on your computer. Attackers use look-alike package names and install scripts. Check the exact name and publisher before npm install or pip install.
check: Codex suggests the command npm install expresss, with three s at the end. What do you check first, and what would make you stop even if the command works?
rubric: Spells the package name from the project's official documentation or repository and compares it letter by letter with the suggested command (expresss against express).
Looks the name up with npm view <name> (or the package page on PyPI) and checks the publisher, the repository link and the age: a look-alike name can exist as a real package.

Stops when the name is new, has few users or has no repository link, and says whether dependency install scripts run in the npm version in use (blocked by default from npm 12, run by default in npm 11).
try: You need npm, which comes with Node.js. Run npm view express name version repository.url: a real, popular package shows its name, a version and a link to its source repository. Then run npm view this-package-does-not-exist-98765: npm prints a 404 error. A package name suggested by an AI can be invented in the same way, and an attacker can register an invented name. A look-alike name may also exist: compare its version, repository link and description with the real package. Finally run npm --version and note whether it is 12 or higher.
pitfall: Wrong belief: installing a package only downloads files. Correct: some packages run install scripts on your computer. npm 12 skips dependency install scripts until you approve them with npm approve-scripts, but npm 11 still runs them by default, so check your npm version and read what you approve.

title: Personal data and privacy
plain: Personal data is any information about an identifiable person: a name, e-mail address, phone number, ID number or health fact. Laws such as the GDPR and Turkey's KVKK limit how you may use it.
check: A friend gives you a spreadsheet of 200 customers with names, e-mail addresses and phone numbers, to build a mailing tool. What do you ask before you open it in your project, and what do you use while learning?
rubric: Marks each column of a sample spreadsheet as personal data or not, including indirect identifiers such as an IP address or a birth date.
Says that with real people's data you ask the data owner first, collect only what you need, and keep it out of Git, chat and AI prompts.
Replaces the real data with made-up rows, using e-mail addresses that end in @example.com.
try: In a scratch folder create sample-people.csv with the header line name,email,city and three rows of made-up people. End every e-mail address with @example.com, a domain reserved for examples that belongs to no real person. Open the file in a text editor: you should see four lines and no real person.
pitfall: Wrong belief: personal data is safe to use if it stays in a private repository or on my own computer. Correct: the rules depend on what you do with data about real people, not on where it is stored, and pasting it into an AI chat sends it to another company. These are basics, not legal advice.
